clue.text: Kingship deliberately lost, they say

indicators.note: they say points to what people speak aloud rather than what is written

blocks.note: the throne stands for royal power

explanation.surface: A king gave up his crown on purpose, so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits in the middle of the clue, with the indicator coming last.
explanation.definitionFit: A match that was thrown was lost on purpose, usually for a bribe.

clue.text: Bath's the place for this drunkard

blocks.note: first meaning: the soft thing you wash with in the tub
second meaning: a heavy drinker who soaks it up

explanation.surface: The spa town of Bath seems just the place for a toper to drink the waters.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is a famous English spa city, which makes it read as a destination; here it is just a bath tub.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponge lives by the tub for washing, and slang calls a heavy drinker a sponge because they soak up liquor.

clue.text: Tricky, overspent outcome?

indicators.note: an outcome is what something turns into, so the preceding letters come out in a new form

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of the two words

explanation.surface: An awkward result for someone who has spent too much.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the letters of the first two words are rearranged, and the clue as a whole describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has spent far beyond their means ends up penniless, which is extremely poor or destitute.

clue.text: They might have set features in Daily Telegraph office

definitions.text: They might have set features in Daily Telegraph office

blocks.note: surface reading: people with fixed, rigid faces

blocks.clueFragment: set features in Daily Telegraph office
blocks.note: setter's reading: newspaper staff who arrange and commission regular articles

explanation.walkthrough: 'Set features' sounds like a stern face; on a newspaper, features are articles that the paper's staff put in place.
explanation.definitionFit: On a newspaper the people who choose, commission and prepare articles for print hold these posts.

clue.text: Hysteric Pat hops off—to see him?

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer to the person one goes to see, rather than a synonym

indicators.note: off can mean wrong or out of order, so the letters before it are shuffled

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A hysterical Pat dashes off to visit someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a hysterical person would be sent to see a PSYCHOTHERAPIST, so the clue points at him.
explanation.definitionFit: A therapist treating mental and emotional disorders is the professional a person in hysterics might be sent to consult.

clue.text: Ravel, for instance, here — settle, ready to start

indicators.note: to start asks for only the opening letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: to compose oneself is to settle down
the opening letter of ready

explanation.surface: Someone is told to calm down and get set to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ravel' looks like a verb, to tangle; it is Maurice Ravel, the French composer of Boléro.
explanation.definitionFit: Maurice Ravel wrote music, so he is an example of a person who writes musical works.

clue.text: Quarter current required for Shelley's herald of spring

blocks.note: one of the four compass quarters
a current of air

explanation.surface: A district needs electricity, like a herald of the season in a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Shelley's 'Ode to the West Wind' ends 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?'
explanation.definitionFit: In Shelley's ode the autumn gale is a prophecy that spring will follow winter.

clue.text: Opal dish damaged in cargo

indicators.note: a damaged dish is broken into pieces, so the letters before it get rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters of both words together

explanation.surface: A precious opal dish arrives broken among the goods in a ship's hold.
explanation.definitionFit: A shipload is the full amount a vessel carries, which is its cargo.

clue.text: One who makes airways tarry?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who holds up air routes, making flights tarry or linger
setter's reading: the airways are the windpipe and lungs, coated with tar

explanation.surface: Someone seems to be delaying flights along the air routes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tarry' looks like the verb meaning linger; it is the adjective, coated in tar, and the airways are the breathing passages of a SMOKER.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobacco tar builds up in the lungs and bronchial passages of a person who regularly inhales cigarette fumes.

clue.text: Chile announced inclusion in heraldic yearbook

definitions.note: read aloud, Chile is 'chilly', which is what the answer means

indicators.note: something included in a phrase sits inside it, so the letters are found running across these words

blocks.note: the end of heraldic and the start of yearbook

explanation.surface: The Chilean entry is noted in a book of coats of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is itself spoken: say 'Chile' and you hear 'chilly', which ICY means.
explanation.definitionFit: Icy weather is very cold, the same as chilly, so the spoken form of the country gives a synonym.

clue.text: Now a debt is settled, players can begin with it

indicators.note: settled can mean put in order or arranged, so the letters before it are arranged afresh

blocks.note: the letters of all three words

explanation.surface: With money matters paid off, the gamblers can start their game.
explanation.walkthrough: The players are musicians, not gamers: a conductor's DOWNBEAT starts them off.
explanation.definitionFit: The downbeat is the conductor's downward stroke marking the first beat of a bar, the signal an orchestra starts on.

clue.text: Heads of Rome

blocks.note: surface reading: the leaders or chiefs of the Roman state
setter's reading: the word for heads in the language of Rome, Latin

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like Roman rulers, but it asks for the Latin plural of caput, a head, familiar from 'per capita'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin caput means head and its plural form is the word familiar from per capita, meaning per head.

clue.text: Excessive devotion to one's own line

definitions.text: Excessive devotion to one's own line

blocks.clueFragment: Excessive devotion to one's own line
blocks.note: surface reading: someone too attached to their own policy or party line
setter's reading: line as lineage, the family tree of forebears

explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' suggests a party line or a line of argument; here it is a family line, and the devotion is literal religious veneration.
explanation.definitionFit: Some religions venerate deceased forebears, honouring the family lineage, which reads as an extreme loyalty to one's descent.

clue.text: Catch in Franco-German alliance

indicators.note: in tells us the letters lie inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the end of Franco and the start of German

explanation.surface: A snag turns up in a treaty between France and Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: A cog is a tooth on a wheel that engages and holds another part, acting as a catch in machinery.

clue.text: Was it a comfort to curate at breakfast?

definitions.text: Was it a comfort to curate at breakfast?

blocks.clueFragment: Was it a comfort to curate at breakfast?
blocks.note: surface reading: something that consoled a young clergyman over his morning meal
setter's reading: the curate's egg, from the old cartoon where a curate calls his bad egg good in parts, needs keeping warm

explanation.walkthrough: A 'curate's egg' is a British byword for something mixed, from a Punch cartoon of a curate politely praising a stale egg; the comfort is a little warm cover for the egg.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg cosy is a small padded cover that keeps a boiled egg warm at the breakfast table.

clue.text: 10s. 6d. to attend ball? Some control needed here!

indicators.note: ten shillings and sixpence was half a guinea, so we keep half the letters of that coin's name

blocks.note: half of guinea, the old coin worth 21 shillings
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Half a guinea to get into a ball, where some supervision is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: In old British money a guinea was 21 shillings, so 10s. 6d. (ten shillings and sixpence) was half a guinea, and half the word guinea is its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Guidance is direction and steering from someone in charge, a form of control.

clue.text: Fare for Tom can include the lights

blocks.note: surface reading: food or a ticket price for a man called Tom
setter's reading: a tom is a male cat, and offal like lungs, called lights, was sold as its food

explanation.walkthrough: A tom is a male cat. Lights are animal lungs, offal once sold by street vendors as food for cats.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap meat and offal sold for feeding pet felines was called by this name in Britain.

clue.text: Tea becoming dear. It is a riddle

indicators.note: becoming means turning into something else, so the word after it changes its order

blocks.note: cha is an informal British word for tea
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that tea is getting expensive, and calls it a mystery.
explanation.definitionFit: A charade is a parlour riddle in which a word is guessed from acted or described syllables.

clue.text: Has been destroyed—what is left?

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so the letters of the word before are rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone surveys the ruins and asks what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: After a fire has destroyed something, the powdery residue that remains is all that survives.

clue.text: Bertie booked, swore to re-form

definitions.note: Bertie as he appears in books, so his surname

indicators.note: to re-form something is to shape it again, so these letters are arranged anew

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Bertie, arrested, vowed to mend his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booked' looks like arrested; it means in books, where P. G. Wodehouse's Bertie appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie Wooster is the foolish gentleman hero of Wodehouse's comic novels, served by his valet Jeeves.

clue.text: Out of date writer? I spot a high error in translation

indicators.note: translation turns words into a different form, so these letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: A translator notices a blunder in an old-fashioned author's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of date' looks like old-fashioned; it means writing about dates that are past.
explanation.definitionFit: A historiographer writes history, so their subject matter is dates and events that have passed.

clue.text: Left a pound in arch over gate

blocks.note: port is the left side of a ship
taken as written
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound

explanation.surface: Someone left a pound coin under the archway of a gate.
explanation.definitionFit: A portal is a grand entrance or doorway, often framed by an arch.

clue.text: The Spanish name in protective coat

indicators.note: in places one word inside another, with the Spanish article wrapping round

blocks.note: el is the Spanish for the
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Spaniard's name is stitched into a protective jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is a hard glossy coating fused onto metal or pottery to protect it.

clue.text: Pitch raincoat on road surface

blocks.note: pitch is a black tarry substance
short for mackintosh, a British raincoat

explanation.surface: Someone throws a raincoat down onto the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' looks like a verb, to throw; it is the noun, a sticky black substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarmac, short for tarmacadam, is the stone and tar mix used to pave roads.

clue.text: Man's powerful partner in play — sure sounds right

blocks.note: surface reading: a strong man's companion in a game
setter's reading: a play title pairing Man with a powerful figure; sure said aloud is the playwright's name, confirming it

explanation.walkthrough: The play is Man and Superman, and 'sure' said in an English accent sounds like Shaw, its author, so the setter is saying Shaw is right.
explanation.definitionFit: In George Bernard Shaw's comedy title, the companion word to Man is the Nietzschean figure of superior power.

clue.text: It was in the bag for the smiling packer

definitions.text: It was in the bag for the smiling packer

blocks.clueFragment: It was in the bag for the smiling packer
blocks.note: surface reading: something was a certainty for a cheerful person packing

blocks.clueFragment: the bag for the smiling packer
blocks.note: setter's reading: the wartime song tells soldiers to pack up their troubles in their old bag of gear and smile

explanation.walkthrough: The First World War song goes 'Pack up your troubles in your old kit-bag, and smile, smile, smile'; 'in the bag' also suggests a sure thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier's kit is his equipment, carried in the canvas bag named after it in the song.

clue.text: Thinly-spread butter and jam

blocks.note: first meaning: a thin smear of butter
second meaning: a tight spot or predicament

explanation.surface: Someone is putting a meagre layer of butter and jam on bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jam' looks like the fruit preserve beside the butter; it is a fix, a predicament.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread and scrape is an old phrase for bread with butter barely spread on, and a tight fix is also called a scrape.

clue.text: Dominating sort doomed to failure in Britain?

definitions.text: Dominating sort doomed to failure in Britain?

blocks.note: surface reading: an overbearing or bossy person
setter's reading: the patriotic song Rule, Britannia promises that Britons never will be held in bondage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule, Britannia' ends each chorus 'Britons never, never, never shall be slaves', so anyone trying to subjugate them must fail.
explanation.definitionFit: An enslaver is someone who subjugates others and holds them in bondage, the most domineering kind of person.
